content: ECHS1, also known as Enoyl Coenzyme A hydratase, short chain, 1, mitochondrial, is a gene found in humans. The protein encoded by this gene plays a critical role in the second step of the mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation pathway. Specifically, it catalyzes the hydration of 2-trans-enoyl-coenzyme A (CoA) intermediates to form L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoAs. The protein product of this gene belongs to the hydratase/isomerase superfamily and is localized within the mitochondrial matrix. Variants of the transcript, which utilize alternative transcription initiation sites, have been documented in scientific literature. The ECHS1 gene spans approximately 11 kilobases (kb) and consists of eight exons. Exon I contains the 5'-untranslated region (UTR), while exon VIII contains the 3'-UTR. Two primary transcription start sites have been identified, located 62 and 63 base pairs upstream of the translation codon, as determined by primer extension analysis. The 5'-flanking region of the ECHS1 gene is rich in guanine and cytosine (GC-rich) and contains multiple SP1 binding motifs. However, it lacks typical TATA or CAAT boxes. Alu repeat elements have been identified within the region spanning -1052 to -770 relative to the cap site, as well as in intron 7. The precursor polypeptide encoded by this gene consists of 290 amino acid residues, including an N-terminal presequence of 29 residues, a 5'-UTR of 21 base pairs, and a 3'-UTR of 391 base pairs. The enzyme enoyl-CoA hydratase (ECH) catalyzes the second step in the beta-oxidation pathway of fatty acid metabolism. This step involves the formation of a β-hydroxyacyl-CoA thioester. Two catalytic glutamic acid residues are thought to work together to activate a water molecule, while the amino acid Glycine-141 is believed to play a role in substrate activation. Additionally, there are two potent inhibitors of ECHS1 that irreversibly inactivate the enzyme through the formation of covalent adducts. ECHS1 has been shown to interact with STAT3, a protein that can function as both an oncogene and a tumor suppressor. ECHS1 specifically represses STAT3 activity by inhibiting its phosphorylation. Furthermore, ECHS1 has been implicated in various cancers, particularly in the development of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Both exogenous and endogenous forms of ECHS1 have been found to bind to hepatitis B surface antigens (HBs), leading to the induction of apoptosis. This suggests that ECHS1 may have potential therapeutic applications in the treatment of patients with hepatitis B virus (HBV)-related hepatitis or HCC.
